extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and practitioners evaluating Section 101/nature-based claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the "markedly different characteristics" analysis under MPEP §2106.04(c) to determine whether a claimed nature-based product is a product-of-nature exception (and thus requires further Step 2A/2B analysis) or is patent-eligible. Covers when to apply the analysis, how to choose counterparts and characteristics, and standards for determining whether differences are "marked."

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and products of nature exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature; court decisions have called these exceptions by various names (e.g., physical phenomena, scientific principles, natural laws, products of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions reflect that basic scientific and technological tools are not patentable (e.g., Funk Bros., Diamond v. Chakrabarty, Parker v. Flook). The Manual lists many court-identified examples (isolated DNA; cloned farm animals; correlations between genetic variations and alleles; metabolic correlations; naturally occurring biomarkers; electromagnetic phenomena; bacterial qualities; primers; chemical principles; cell-free fetal DNA; genotype–drug response relationships). Even if a claim describes a natural ability or quality, it might not recite an exception if it is focused on process steps or treatments (see Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect and examples of treatment claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting a law/natural phenomenon require Step 2A Prong Two analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim recites such an exception, it may still be eligible under Pathways A–C if it integrates the exception into a practical application (e.g., Vanda — genotype-tailored treatment step integrated the natural relationship). If a claim does not recite a law/phenomenon, it is eligible at Pathway B (Step 2A: NO) unless it recites another exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature exception for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law/phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts often refer to the exception as a 'product of nature'. Products of nature include naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from naturally occurring counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2A of the Office eligibility analysis treats 'law of nature' and 'natural phenomenon' as inclusive of 'products of nature'. Examples (Myriad, Ambry, Roslin) show claims to isolated DNA or primers can be products of nature. Non-naturally occurring products (e.g., cloned organisms) are not automatically eligible solely because of human intervention—eligibility depends on whether they possess markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A Prong One and is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions by comparing the claimed nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this analysis only to nature-based product limitations in the claim (not to non-nature elements). Nature-based products include both eligible and ineligible products. If a product has markedly different characteristics, it is not a product of nature (Step 2A: NO) unless another exception is recited; if it lacks such characteristics, it is a product-of-nature exception and requires Prong Two analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform the analysis when the claim includes a nature-based product that is not merely a naturally occurring product in its natural state; do not perform it if the limitation is directed to a naturally occurring product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, it by definition falls under the product-of-nature exception and the analysis is unnecessary. If the product is non-naturally occurring due to human intervention, the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed to determine whether it is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims to a nature-based product by itself, the markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied to the entire claimed product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chakrabarty applied the analysis to the entire claimed bacterium (including added plasmids). When the claim is to a combination of components that together constitute the nature-based product, analyze the resultant combination rather than separate components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to combination and kit claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, analyze the resultant nature-based combination; when a nature-based product is claimed with non-nature elements, analyze only the nature-based limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For a probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk, analyze the mixture as the nature-based product. For a yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus plus container and instructions, analyze the Lactobacillus for markedly different characteristics; evaluate container/instructions as additional elements in Prong Two/Step 2B if the Lactobacillus is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: focus on product characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the markedly different characteristics analysis turns on whether the claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for more on product-by-process claims; the key question is the nature of the claimed product, not the process steps per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims generally not subject to markedly different analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim is generally not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process because process analysis should focus on active steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect — process of creating a preparation of cryopreserved hepatocytes was analyzed as a process, not by comparing hepatocytes used in the steps. However, if a process claim is drafted so that it is substantively no different from a product claim (i.e., effectively focuses on the product), then the markedly different analysis applies to the recited nature-based product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting appropriate natural counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) in its natural state to compare with the claimed nature-based product; choose the closest naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product is derived from a natural thing, the thing from which it was derived is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A compared to acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with surrounding natural matter (e.g., for an isolated gene, the counterpart is the gene, not the whole chromosome). If multiple possible counterparts exist, select the closest one based on examiner expertise; if no single counterpart exists (e.g., cloned animal from two breeds), select the closest counterpart(s). Best practice: if rejecting, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action to aid applicant response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying appropriate characteristics for comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics to compare that are actually possessed by the claimed product as recited in the claim and encompassed by the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics may be explicit in the claim (e.g., chemical name implies structure) or apparent from the BRI (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies nucleotide sequence and encoded protein). Appropriate characteristics may be structural, functional, or other properties and must be possessed by the claimed product (unclaimed characteristics cannot supply eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product’s structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exhaustive categories: biological or pharmacological functions/activities (e.g., protein-encoding information, binding ability), chemical and physical properties (e.g., alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (physical presence of plasmids, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype). The Manual provides specific case examples for each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for determining 'markedly different' characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A characteristic is 'markedly different' if it is changed compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and the change was caused/produced by the inventor and is not merely inherent, innate, or an incidental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show marked difference, the inventor must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic different from the counterpart. Incidental differences (e.g., isolation artifacts) or characteristics inherent to the natural counterpart do not suffice (Myriad). If no change in any characteristic exists, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products having markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products exhibited markedly different characteristics and thus were eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium had additional plasmids and the ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons (changed structural and functional characteristics). Myriad (cDNA): cDNA retained exons but had distinct nucleotide sequence (structural change) and was not a product of nature. These show structural or functional changes caused by inventors can be markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products did not have marked differences and were held to be products of nature (ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated BRCA1/BRCA2 genes lacked marked differences beyond incidental changes from isolation (structurally identical otherwise), so they were products of nature. Isolation alone (removal from surrounding material) is generally an incidental change insufficient to establish marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) considerations and claim breadth issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should consider BRI when determining whether the claim recites a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to a 'cloned giraffe' could, under BRI, encompass cloned giraffes with and without markedly different characteristics. If claim breadth encompasses ineligible embodiments, the claim recites a product of nature and requires Prong Two/Step 2B analysis. If rejected, examiners should point out the BRI and recommend amendments to narrow the claim to eligible embodiments if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner best practices when rejecting on product-of-nature grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting claims as product-of-nature exceptions, the examiner should identify the selected natural counterpart and recommend claim amendments if possible to narrow claim scope to eligible embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying the selected counterpart in the Office action assists applicant responses and clarifies how the examiner interpreted the claim. Pointing out the BRI and recommending amendments to narrow to embodiments not directed to products of nature is a best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews for Step 2B rejections involving tentative abstract ideas (related procedural guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to a Step 2B rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea, an interview with the examiner may be conducted to help advance prosecution and identify eligible subject matter; interviews with the TC Director who approved the tentative abstract idea are not required for withdrawal of the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 713 for interview guidance. If the TC Director approved the tentative abstract idea procedure, an interview with that director is not necessary because the examiner retains authority to withdraw or maintain the §101 rejection on consideration of applicant’s reply; the examiner is not required to obtain TC Director approval to withdraw or maintain such a rejection.
